**Proof.**

Let $G$ be a group, $a \in G$, and let $Z(G) = \{z \in G : zg = gz \text{ for all } g \in G\}$ denote the center of $G$. The centralizer of $a$ is
$$C(a) = \{g \in G : ga = ag\}.$$

We prove both directions.

**($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $a \in Z(G)$.** By definition of the center, $a$ commutes with every element of $G$, i.e., $ag = ga$ for all $g \in G$. Hence every $g \in G$ satisfies the defining condition for membership in $C(a)$, so $G \subseteq C(a)$. Since $C(a) \subseteq G$ trivially (the centralizer is always a subset of $G$), we conclude $C(a) = G$.

**($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $C(a) = G$.** Then every $g \in G$ belongs to $C(a)$, which by definition means $ga = ag$ for every $g \in G$. This is precisely the condition that $a$ commutes with all elements of $G$, i.e., $a \in Z(G)$.

Therefore, $a \in Z(G)$ if and only if $C(a) = G$. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
